submission.natural_language_explanation: Fires on words that describe physical spatial layout, mostly by token identity: compass directions (north, south, northeast, southwest), directional and positional words (toward, towards, outside, inside, across, beside, beneath, atop, front, overlooking), parts and surfaces of buildings and objects (window, floor, door, wall, roof, corner, side, bottom, cabinets, staircase), dimension adjectives (tall, wide, long, narrow, deep, perpendicular) and position verbs (stands, stood, lies, located, situated, parked). These words fire even when used figuratively ('window of opportunity', 'side effects', 'rock bottom'), and plain prepositions (on, in, at, over, near, under, behind, below) and place nouns fire only after such spatial words; text with no physical position, direction or dimension words (abstract, social, financial or narrative text, code, 'lives in London', 'behind the sofa') stays below the line.

Bread is a staple food that has been produced and consumed across multiple cultures for thousands of years. It is often viewed as a symbol of sustenance, community, and life itself. In this essay, we will explore the traditional practices, customs, and beliefs related to bread production in three culturally diverse regions, and examine the significance of bread within their respective societies.

First, let's consider the Middle East. Bread is a crucial component of the Middle Eastern diet, and it is often viewed as a gift from God. In many cultures, the production of bread is steeped in religious significance. For example, in Judaism, the bread known as challah is traditionally made on Friday evening in preparation for the Jewish Sabbath. When the dough is prepared, it is braided with six strands, to represent the six days of the week. In Islam, the month of Ramadan is marked by the production of various types of bread, such as pita or naan, which are eaten after sunset to break the day's fast. Throughout the region, bread-making is often anchored in communal practices, such as the baking of bread in communal ovens or the inclusion of prayers during the bread-making process.

The production of bread in India is similarly steeped in tradition and spirituality. In India, bread is typically made using wheat flour, but can also be made using gram flour or millet flour. Across the country, bread-making is often seen as sacred work, with the consumption of bread viewed as a form of communion with the divine. In some regions of India, bread is made by women as an expression of their devotion to the goddess Annapurna, who is the goddess of food and nourishment. In other regions, the production of bread is seen as a way to honor the deities, with certain types of bread being associated with specific gods or goddesses.

In many families, the process of baking bread is passed down from generation to generation, with recipes and techniques being held onto with a sense of reverence. WASHINGTON, D.C. – Rep. Scott Tipton, R-Cortez, addressed concerned listeners on multiple issues during a telephone town hall Monday evening.
Most callers said they were worried about potential changes in health care policies. Asked about Medicaid coverage, Tipton assured residents of Colorado’s 3rd Congressional District that those who qualified would keep their coverage.
But both the House and the Senate bills would phase out the Medicaid expansion program. The Affordable Care Act increased the income limit for those receiving Medicaid in some states. The expansion increased the number of recipients by 11 million. The proposed bills would curtail federal coverage and would result in the loss of coverage for people above a lowered income cap. Medicaid covers one in five Americans and is the nation’s largest single health insurer.
Callers also voiced anxiety on coverage of pre-existing conditions. Tipton said no one wants people with pre-existing conditions to be uninsured.
“Irrespective of politics, we all want to make sure people with pre-existing conditions are covered,” Tipton said.
The Congressional Budget Office predicts the House bill would cause 23 million people to lose coverage, while the Senate bill would cause 22 million to lose coverage.
Other callers brought up issues such water rights, the opioid crisis in the state, free choice of education, and legislation in favor of small businesses.
Small businessesSome callers asked Tipton about his promises and goals for small Colorado businesses.
Tipton said he is trying to drop the corporate tax from 35 percent to 15 percent. The United States’ corporate tax rate is the highest in the world, and nearly half of Colorado’s workforce is employed by small businesses, according to a report by the U.S. Small Business Administration. Tipton said his district has a harder time economically than other districts.
Water rightsTipton said he is working on water legislation this week and plans to introduce The Water Protection Act. The bill would prevent the federal government from taking private water rights from farmers, ranchers and ski resorts without compensation.
Opioid crisisMultiple callers asked about Tipton’s commitment to addressing the opioid crisis and providing treatment. Colorado received a $7.8 million grant for opioid treatment and prevention in May from the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. A state press release said the money will be allocated for programs like medication-assisted therapy, family therapy, overdose reversal medications and partnerships with law enforcement.
“In terms of trying to treat the addiction, this is something that is going to take a committed effort, not only in our community, but resources from the federal government and out of our state as well,” Tipton said.
The Congressman said more than 60,000 people signed up to participate in the telephone town hall.

1941 Texas hurricane

The 1941 Texas hurricane, the second storm of the 1941 Atlantic hurricane season, was a large and intense tropical cyclone that struck coastal Texas as a major hurricane in September 1941, causing relatively severe damage. The storm is estimated to have formed in the eastern Gulf of Mexico on September 16. After attaining hurricane strength, it completed a clockwise loop and turned northwestward. The hurricane continued to strengthen until it made landfall near East Matagorda Bay, Texas, with winds of 125 miles per hour (201 km / h), but rapidly weakened as it headed inland. Damage from the storm amounted to about $6.5 million, and crops throughout the region were largely destroyed. The city of Houston suffered extensive damage as the storm passed to the east. The hurricane disrupted activities related to the Louisiana Maneuvers. Later, the system became extratropical and passed over Lake Huron, killing three people in Toronto. Overall, seven people lost their lives due to the cyclone.

Meteorological history

In the middle of September, disturbed atmospheric conditions from a trough or tropical wave existed over the western Caribbean Sea and gradually coalesced near western Cuba on September 15 – 16. Even so, surrounding surface weather observations did not suggest that an area of low pressure had generated, but gradual organization continued until a tropical depression formed on September 17 in the central Gulf of Mexico about 120 miles (193 km) north of the Yucatán Peninsula. Operationally, the United States Weather Bureau failed to detect a tropical cyclone in the Gulf of Mexico until a day later. After formation, the system initially moved northwestward, a heading that continued early on September 18. At that time, the system became a tropical storm more than 300 mi (483 km) to the south-southeast of New Orleans, Louisiana.

Over the next three days, the intensifying storm executed a gradual clockwise loop, moving to the south-southeast before turning back to the west. After intensifying into a hurricane on September 21, the storm began assuming a more northwestward course, toward the Texas Gulf Coast. It continued to strengthen into a major hurricane, peaking at 125 miles per hour (201 km / h) late on September 23. Just afterward, the storm went ashore east of Bay City, Texas, at peak intensity with an estimated central pressure of 942 millibars (27.82 inHg). However, few weather instruments were sited close to the point of landfall, so the lowest recorded pressure on land was only 970.5 mb (28.66 inHg) in Houston. After landfall, the cyclone curved to the northeast and passed just west of Houston early on September 24. It accelerated as it continued to move inland and transitioned into an extratropical storm on September 25. The post-tropical system dissipated early on September 27 over northeastern Quebec, near the Torngat Mountains National Park.
